probabilityNote: Probability is an estimate of how likely a question is, based on common patterns in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers and the weight of each topic in the syllabus. It is not a promise.

questions.question: Define misbranded, adulterated and spurious drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Discuss the penalties for manufacture and sale of such drugs as amended in 2008.
questions.answer:
1. Introduction: D&C Act 1940 regulates import, manufacture, distribution and sale; sections 17, 17A, 17B define the three categories.
2. Misbranded (s.17): coloured, coated, powdered or polished to conceal damage or look better; not labelled as prescribed; label or container carries a false or misleading claim.
3. Adulterated (s.17A): filthy, putrid or decomposed substance; made, packed or stored in insanitary conditions; container of poisonous substance; non-permitted colour; harmful or toxic substance; substance mixed to reduce quality or strength.
4. Spurious (s.17B): sold under the name of another drug (imitation/substitute); pretends to be the product of another maker; fictitious manufacturer; substituted wholly or partly; claims to be product of a maker who did not make it.
5. Section 18 prohibits manufacture, sale, stocking and distribution of such drugs.
6. Penalties (s.27 after 2008): (a) adulterated/spurious drug likely to cause death or grievous hurt — 10 years to life, fine not less than ₹10 lakh or 3× value of drugs confiscated, paid as compensation to victim/relatives; (b) adulterated drug or no licence — 3–5 years, fine ≥ ₹1 lakh or 3× value; (c) spurious drug — 7 years to life, fine ≥ ₹3 lakh or 3× value; (d) other contraventions — 1–2 years, fine ≥ ₹20,000.
7. Other features: offences under 27(a) and (c) cognizable and non-bailable; special courts; prosecution by inspector, gazetted officer, aggrieved person or consumer association; repeat offences (s.30) heavier; compounding (s.32B), widened by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023.
8. Conclusion: confiscation of stock and cancellation of licence also follow.

questions.question: Describe the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules regarding import of drugs: classes of drugs prohibited from import, import under licence or permit, and offences.
questions.answer:
1. Authority: Central Licensing Authority (DCGI, CDSCO); port offices check consignments.
2. Classes prohibited (s.10): not of standard quality; misbranded, adulterated, spurious; patent/proprietary medicine without true formula on label; drug claiming to cure Schedule J diseases; harmful cosmetic; drugs prohibited in country of origin or by rules; import without licence.
3. Section 10A: Government may prohibit import of drugs involving risk or lacking claimed therapeutic value; import of cosmetics tested on animals also prohibited.
4. Import under licence: registration certificate of foreign manufacturer and product; import licence for drugs other than Schedule X; separate licence for Schedule X; test licence for examination, test or analysis; small quantities for a patient's personal use with prescription; new drugs and clinical trial material under NDCT Rules 2019; devices under Medical Devices Rules 2017.
5. Conditions: proper premises and storage, manufacturer's test report with each consignment, minimum residual shelf life, allow inspection, keep records, report changes.
6. Offences (s.13): import of spurious/adulterated drugs — imprisonment and fine (heavier); other contraventions — lighter penalty, compoundable under s.32B; repeat offences higher; goods confiscated (s.14).
7. Note: form numbers and amounts are revised often; check the current rules.

questions.question: Explain the conditions for grant of a licence to manufacture drugs and the conditions of the licence. Add notes on loan licence and repacking licence.
questions.answer:
1. Licensing authority: State Licensing Authority; Central Licence Approving Authority (DCGI) for Schedule C/C(1), LVPs, vaccines, sera, blood products.
2. Licence types: 25 (drugs other than C, C1, X), 28 (C and C1), 25A/28A loan, 25B repacking, 29 test.
3. Conditions for grant: premises, plant and equipment as per Schedule M; manufacture under active direction of qualified technical staff (degree in pharmacy/pharmaceutical chemistry/chemistry with experience); independent QC department with qualified analyst and laboratory; storage facilities; inspection before grant.
4. Conditions of licence: keep Schedule U records; test every batch; keep reference samples; allow inspection and sampling; report changes; recall substandard batches; comply with Schedule M; pay retention fee (licences no longer lapse after a fixed term).
5. Loan licence: given to a person without own factory who uses premises, equipment and staff of a licensed manufacturer; host must have spare capacity and agree; both responsible for quality.
6. Repacking licence: breaking bulk into small packs for retail; suitable premises; competent person; correct labels with original maker's details and batch; records; some categories excluded.

questions.question: Write the objectives of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
questions.answer:
1. Regulate import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs and cosmetics through licences.
2. Ensure drugs and cosmetics are safe, effective and of standard quality.
3. Prevent sale of substandard, misbranded, adulterated and spurious products.
4. Regulate Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and homoeopathic drugs.
5. Set up DTAB, DCC, CDL and similar ASU bodies.
6. Provide for inspectors, government analysts, offences and penalties.
7. Based on the recommendations of the Drugs Enquiry Committee (1930–31).

questions.question: Give the legal definitions of the schedules to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules (any ten).
questions.answer:
Act: First Schedule — authoritative ASU books; Second Schedule — standards for drugs.
Rules: A — forms; B — fees for testing; C/C(1) — biological and special products; D — import exemptions; E(1) — poisonous ASU substances; F — biologicals and (Part XII B) blood centres; G — use under medical supervision; H/H1 — prescription drugs; J — diseases no drug may claim to cure; K — exemptions; M — GMP; N — pharmacy equipment; O — disinfectant fluids; P/P1 — shelf life/pack sizes; Q — coal tar colours for cosmetics; R — mechanical contraceptives; S — cosmetic standards; T — ASU GMP; U — manufacturing and analytical records; V — standards for patent medicines; X — high-misuse drugs; Y — clinical trials (now NDCT Rules 2019).

questions.question: What is meant by manufacture of a drug for examination, test or analysis? Write the conditions of such a licence.
questions.answer:
1. Licence (traditionally Form 29) to make small quantities of a drug for research, development, stability studies or trial supply.
2. Conditions: drug not to be sold; quantities limited to need; for a stated period; under a qualified person; records of production, use and disposal kept and shown to inspectors; premises and equipment suitable; licensing authority informed of results where required; unused material destroyed properly.
3. Different from manufacture of a new drug, which needs permission of the Central Licensing Authority under NDCT Rules 2019 before commercial manufacture.

questions.question: Write a note on the prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs, including section 26A.
questions.answer:
1. Section 18 prohibits manufacture for sale, sale, stocking, exhibiting or distribution of: drugs or cosmetics not of standard quality, misbranded, adulterated or spurious; patent/proprietary medicines without true formula; drugs claiming to cure Schedule J diseases; products made in breach of the Act; products without licence.
2. Section 26A: Central Government, after consulting DTAB, may regulate, restrict or prohibit a drug or cosmetic that involves risk to humans or animals, lacks claimed therapeutic value or has no therapeutic justification for its ingredients (used to ban irrational FDCs).
3. Section 26B (2008): regulate or restrict a drug in emergencies like epidemics or natural calamities.
4. Breach punishable under section 27.

questions.question: Define a spurious drug.
questions.answer: A drug sold under the name of another drug, or imitating it; or pretending to be the product of a manufacturer who did not make it; or bearing a fictitious maker's name; or substituted wholly or partly by another drug (section 17B, D&C Act).

questions.question: What is a loan licence?
questions.answer: A manufacturing licence (Form 25A/28A) given to a person who has no factory of his own but uses the premises, equipment and technical staff of another licensed manufacturer to make his products.

questions.question: Discuss Schedules G, H, H1 and X of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules with their labelling and record requirements.
questions.answer:
1. Schedule G: drugs to be used under medical supervision (e.g. some antihistamines, oral antidiabetics); label 'Caution: It is dangerous to take this preparation except under medical supervision'.
2. Schedule H: prescription drugs (antibiotics, antihypertensives, steroids); label Rx + 'Schedule H drug – Warning: To be sold by retail on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner only'; NRx if also under NDPS; sale only on prescription, quantity as prescribed, prescription stamped, sale details recorded.
3. Schedule H1 (2013, in force 2014): 3rd/4th generation antibiotics, anti-TB drugs, some habit-forming drugs; Rx in red with boxed warning in red border; separate register with prescriber, patient, drug and quantity kept 3 years; aim to curb antimicrobial resistance.
4. Schedule X: high-misuse narcotic/psychotropic drugs (amphetamine, methylphenidate, some barbiturates); label XRx in red; special licences; prescription in duplicate, one copy kept 2 years; separate records; storage under lock and key.
5. Conclusion: breaches punishable under section 27(d); licence may be suspended.

questions.question: Describe the administration of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act: DTAB, DCC, CDL, government analysts, licensing authorities and drugs inspectors.
questions.answer:
1. DTAB (s.5): technical advice to Central and State Governments; ex officio members (DGHS as chairman, DCGI, Director CDL Kolkata, Director CRI Kasauli, Director IVRI Izatnagar, President PCI and others), nominated members (State drug control officers, industry), elected members (pharmacy teacher by PCI, medicine teacher, pharmacologist by ICMR, professional associations); 3-year term.
2. DCC (s.7): 2 representatives of Central Government + 1 of each State; ensures uniform administration.
3. CDL (s.6): Kolkata; tests samples, appellate (referee) testing — report final; standards.
4. Government Analysts (s.20): qualified, no financial interest; analyse samples and report.
5. Licensing authorities: DCGI for import, new drugs, C/C1 approval; State Drugs Controller for manufacture and sale licences; controlling authority supervises inspectors.
6. Drugs inspectors (s.21–23): qualifications as per rules, no financial interest; powers — inspect, take samples (pay price, divide into four portions), search, stop vehicles, seize, examine records; duties — regular inspection, sampling, complaints, prosecution with sanction.

questions.question: Describe the different types of licences for sale of drugs and the conditions for grant of retail and wholesale licences. Add a note on restricted licence.
questions.answer:
1. Licences: 20 retail (other than C, C1, X), 21 retail (C, C1), 20B/21B wholesale, 20F/20G Schedule X retail/wholesale, 20A/21A restricted. Granted by State Licensing Authority.
2. Retail conditions: premises at least 10 m² (15 m² combined retail and wholesale); clean storage; refrigerator for cold-chain items; sale under personal supervision of registered pharmacist; H, H1, X drugs only on prescription with records; licence displayed; expired stock separated.
3. Wholesale conditions: adequate premises and storage; competent person in charge (registered pharmacist, or graduate with 1 year experience, or SSC with 4 years experience in drug trade); sales only to licensed parties, hospitals, RMPs with invoices showing batch and expiry.
4. Restricted licence: for dealers without pharmacist, usually in villages and itinerant vendors; only listed household remedies in original sealed packs; no dispensing.
5. Penalties: section 27; licence suspension or cancellation.

questions.question: Write a note on Schedule M.
questions.answer:
1. Lays down Good Manufacturing Practices and requirements of premises, plant and equipment.
2. Revised Schedule M notified December 2023 (G.S.R. 922(E)), aligned with WHO GMP.
3. Covers pharmaceutical quality system, quality risk management, product quality review, personnel, premises, equipment, sanitation, materials, documentation, production, QC, validation, complaints, recalls, self-inspection, contract work.
4. Separate parts for each dosage form (sterile, oral solid, liquid, topical, API, biologicals).
5. Compliance is a condition of manufacturing licence; MSMEs given extended time.

questions.question: Write the requirements of Schedule N.
questions.answer: Minimum equipment for a pharmacy: premises separate from living quarters, clean, ventilated, adequate area, dispensing area closed to public; equipment such as balances and weights, measures, mortars and pestles, spatulas, funnels, water bath, refrigerator, ointment slab, suppository mould; books — current IP, National Formulary of India, D&C Act and Rules; registered pharmacist in charge of compounding and dispensing; materials and containers as needed.

questions.question: What are the general labelling requirements for drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules?
questions.answer: Label on innermost container and covering must show: proper (generic) name more prominent than brand; net content; active ingredients per unit; manufacturer's name and address; batch number; manufacturing licence number; dates of manufacture and expiry; MRP; schedule symbols and warnings (Rx, NRx, XRx, caution); 'For external use only' or 'Not for injection' where needed; storage conditions; for injections route and preservative. Special labels for veterinary drugs, physician's samples, Government supply and ASU drugs. Only permitted colours may be used.

questions.question: Write a note on Schedule Y and the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019.
questions.answer:
1. Schedule Y gave requirements for clinical trials and permission to import or manufacture new drugs.
2. Since 2019, NDCT Rules replace Part XA and Schedule Y for new drugs and trials.
3. Features: Central Licensing Authority (DCGI) permission; registered ethics committees; informed consent (audio-video in specified cases); timelines for approval; compensation for trial injury or death; serious adverse event reporting; rules for academic trials and waiver of local trials.
4. Phases I–IV: safety in volunteers, dose finding, confirmatory efficacy, post-marketing surveillance.

questions.question: What is the composition of the Drugs Consultative Committee?
questions.answer: Two representatives of the Central Government and one representative of each State Government (section 7); it secures uniformity in administration of the Act.

questions.question: What is the minimum area for a retail drug store?
questions.answer: At least 10 square metres for retail sale; at least 15 square metres where retail and wholesale are carried on together.

questions.question: Describe the constitution and functions of the Pharmacy Council of India under the Pharmacy Act, 1948.
questions.answer:
1. Pharmacy Act 1948 — objectives: regulate profession, set up PCI and State Councils, education standards, registration.
2. Constitution (s.3): (a) 6 members elected by UGC from pharmacy teachers, at least one each in pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacy, pharmacology, pharmacognosy; (b) 6 nominated by Central Govt, at least 4 qualified in pharmacy/pharmaceutical chemistry; (c) 1 elected by MCI (now NMC); (d) DGHS ex officio; (dd) Drugs Controller of India ex officio; (e) Director CDL ex officio; (f) 1 representative each of UGC and AICTE; (g) 1 registered pharmacist elected by each State Council; (h) 1 member nominated by each State Govt (registered pharmacist).
3. President and Vice-President elected from members; term generally 5 years; Executive Committee.
4. Functions: Education Regulations (s.10) — period and nature of study, subjects, practical training, equipment, admission; approval of courses/institutions (s.12); withdrawal (s.13); inspection; recognition of foreign qualifications (s.14); Central Register (s.15A); Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015; advising Government.

questions.question: Discuss the NDPS Act, 1985 with respect to objectives, important definitions, the Consultative Committee and the National Fund for Control of Drug Abuse.
questions.answer:
1. Objectives: consolidate law; stringent control of operations; forfeiture of property; implement UN conventions; medical and scientific use only.
2. Definitions: addict; cannabis (charas, ganja, mixtures); coca derivative; opium; opium derivative; poppy straw; manufactured drug; narcotic drug (coca leaf, cannabis, opium, poppy straw, manufactured drugs); psychotropic substance (Schedule list); essential narcotic drug (2014); small/commercial quantity (notified); controlled substance.
3. Authorities: s.4 Central Govt (NCB 1986), s.5 Narcotics Commissioner, s.7 State officers.
4. Consultative Committee (s.6): chairman + up to 20 members appointed by Central Govt; advises on administration; may form sub-committees with non-members; meets as required.
5. National Fund (s.7A, 1989): from sale of forfeited property, grants, investment income; used to combat illicit traffic, control abuse, identify/treat/rehabilitate addicts, prevent abuse, educate public, supply drugs to addicts where medically needed.
6. Conclusion: punishments graded by quantity; s.64A immunity for addicts seeking treatment.

questions.question: Explain the provisions of the NDPS Act relating to opium poppy cultivation, production of poppy straw, manufacture, sale and export of opium, and the offences and penalties.
questions.answer:
1. s.8 prohibits cultivation except as permitted; s.9 Central powers over opium poppy and opium; s.10 State powers over poppy straw.
2. Cultivation: notified tracts in MP, Rajasthan, UP; licences by Narcotics Commissioner; all opium tendered to CBN at fixed price; minimum yield to retain licence; embezzlement punishable (s.19).
3. Poppy straw: controlled after harvest; possession, transport, sale under State licence; concentrate of poppy straw under strict control.
4. Manufacture: opium and alkaloids at Government Opium and Alkaloid Works (Ghazipur, Neemuch); sale to licensed manufacturers controlled; export only by or for Central Govt under import certificates.
5. Offences s.15–22 by substance; graded punishment: small — RI up to 1 year or fine up to ₹10,000 or both; intermediate — up to 10 years + fine up to ₹1 lakh; commercial — 10–20 years + fine ₹1–2 lakh.
6. Others: s.27 consumption; s.27A financing (10–20 years); s.29 abetment/conspiracy; s.31 repeat 1.5×; s.31A death penalty (discretionary since 2014); s.35 presumption; s.37 bail restrictions; forfeiture of property.

questions.question: Write the constitution and functions of a State Pharmacy Council.
questions.answer: Constitution (s.19): 6 elected by registered pharmacists; 5 nominated by State Govt (at least 3 pharmacy qualified); 1 elected by State Medical Council; chief administrative medical officer, officer in charge of drugs control and Government Analyst (ex officio). Joint State Council possible under s.20. Functions: maintain register of pharmacists; register qualified persons and issue certificates; remove/restore names; appoint registrar and inspectors (s.26A); maintain discipline; continuing education.

questions.question: Write the procedure and qualifications for registration of pharmacists under the Pharmacy Act.
questions.answer:
1. First register (s.29–31) prepared when Act applied, entering persons with listed qualifications or experience.
2. Subsequent registration (s.32): age 18 or above; approved qualification under Education Regulations (D.Pharm/B.Pharm etc.); prescribed fee; application to State Council; certificate issued.
3. Renewal fees (s.34); name removed for non-payment.
4. Removal (s.36) for misconduct, conviction or wrong entry after inquiry; restoration (s.37).
5. Offences: s.41 falsely claiming registration; s.42 unregistered dispensing; s.43 not surrendering certificate — penalties revised by Jan Vishwas Act 2023 (from 31 Dec 2024) with adjudication under new s.43A.

questions.question: Distinguish between manufacture in bond and outside bond under the Medicinal and Toilet Preparations Act, 1955. What is the present status of this Act?
questions.answer: In bond: alcohol supplied without duty; duty paid when finished goods removed; constant excise officer supervision; compulsory for restricted preparations capable of being consumed as alcoholic beverages. Outside bond: maker uses duty-paid alcohol; periodic supervision; for unrestricted preparations not capable of being drunk as beverages. Export possible without duty or with rebate. Status: repealed by section 174 of the CGST Act, 2017, from 1 July 2017; alcohol-based preparations now taxed under GST.

questions.question: Write the objectives and important definitions of the Medicinal and Toilet Preparations Act, 1955.
questions.answer: Objectives: levy and collect excise duty on medicinal and toilet preparations containing alcohol, opium, Indian hemp or other narcotics; uniform duty in India; prevent misuse of duty-free alcohol through supervised manufacture. Definitions: alcohol (ethyl alcohol C2H5OH of any strength); dutiable goods (in the Schedule); medicinal preparation (remedy or prescription for internal/external use including Ayurvedic, homoeopathic, allopathic); toilet preparation (for toilet of body or perfumery); narcotic drug; bonded manufactory. Note: repealed by CGST Act 2017, s.174, from 1 July 2017.

questions.question: Define 'manufactured drug' under the NDPS Act.
questions.answer: Coca derivatives, medicinal hemp, opium derivatives, poppy straw concentrate and any other narcotic substance or preparation declared to be a manufactured drug by the Central Government.

questions.question: What is section 64A of the NDPS Act?
questions.answer: It gives immunity from prosecution to an addict charged with consumption or a small-quantity offence who voluntarily seeks treatment for de-addiction at a recognised hospital or institution.

questions.question: Discuss the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 with respect to objectives, definitions, prohibited advertisements, exempted advertisements and penalties.
questions.answer:
1. Objectives: control drug advertisements; prohibit adverts of magic remedies; prevent self-medication and quackery.
2. Definitions: advertisement (any notice, circular, label, wrapper, document, oral or light/sound/smoke announcement); drug; magic remedy (talisman, mantra, kavacha, charm claiming miraculous powers); RMP; taking part in publication.
3. Prohibited (s.3): adverts suggesting use for procuring miscarriage or preventing conception, improving sexual pleasure, correcting menstrual disorders, or treating any of the 54 Schedule diseases (cancer, diabetes, epilepsy, cataract, glaucoma, leucoderma, venereal diseases etc.).
4. s.4 misleading/false adverts; s.5 magic remedies; s.6 import/export of such documents.
5. Exemptions (s.14): RMP signboard; scientific/social treatise; adverts sent confidentially to RMPs, hospitals, laboratories; Government adverts or with its sanction; others notified.
6. Powers: s.8 entry, search and seizure by authorised gazetted officer.
7. Penalty (s.7): first conviction up to 6 months or fine or both; subsequent up to 1 year or fine or both; company officers liable. A 2020 draft amendment proposed higher penalties; check status.

questions.question: Describe the provisions of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 relating to experiments on animals and the CPCSEA guidelines.
questions.answer:
1. Objectives: prevent unnecessary pain; Animal Welfare Board; control experiments.
2. Definitions: animal (any living creature other than human), captive animal, domestic animal, experiment.
3. Chapter IV: s.14 experiments lawful for advancement of knowledge; s.15 Committee (CPCSEA, renamed CCSEA in 2023); s.17 duties and rules; s.18 inspection; s.19 power to prohibit experiments, suspend or revoke registration; s.20 penalty.
4. Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control and Supervision) Rules 1998: registration of breeders and users.
5. IAEC: biological scientist, scientists of different disciplines, veterinarian, scientist in charge of animal house, outside scientist, socially aware non-scientist, Committee's main and link nominees; approves small-animal protocols, refers large-animal ones.
6. Breeding/stocking: species-wise areas, controlled environment, caging, diet, quarantine, veterinary care, trained staff, animals from registered breeders.
7. Experiments: 3 Rs + rehabilitation; trained persons; lowest suitable species; anaesthesia/analgesia; humane euthanasia.
8. Transfer/acquisition from registered establishments with records; records of animals and protocols; penalties under s.20.

questions.question: Explain DPCO 2013 with respect to objectives, important definitions, calculation of ceiling price of scheduled formulations, retail price of new drugs and NLEM.
questions.answer:
1. Issued under s.3 of Essential Commodities Act 1955, based on NPPP 2012; enforced by NPPA (1997); replaced DPCO 1995; market-based pricing.
2. Objectives: essential medicines at reasonable prices; room for innovation and competition; avoid shortages.
3. Definitions: scheduled formulation, non-scheduled formulation, ceiling price, MRP, retail price, price to retailer, moving annual turnover, new drug, bulk drug, WPI.
4. Ceiling price: brands with ≥1% market share → simple average PTR → + 16% retailer margin. Example: PTRs 20, 24, 16 → average 20 → ceiling 23.20.
5. Manufacturers above ceiling reduce; below must not increase except WPI revision every 1 April (para 16).
6. Retail price of new drug fixed by Government on application before launch.
7. Non-scheduled: MRP rise ≤ 10% in 12 months; para 19 extraordinary circumstances; six months' notice to discontinue; overcharging recovered with interest; bulk drugs not routinely price-controlled.
8. NLEM 2022: 384 medicines in 27 categories, generic names, = First Schedule of DPCO.

questions.question: Write the composition and functions of the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC).
questions.answer: Composition: biological scientist, two scientists from different biological disciplines, veterinarian, scientist in charge of animal facility, scientist from outside the institute, socially aware non-scientific member, and the Committee's (CPCSEA/CCSEA) main and link nominees. Functions: review and approve protocols on small animals; refer large-animal protocols to the Committee; check justification of numbers and species; ensure anaesthesia, analgesia and humane end points; inspect animal house; maintain records; report to the Committee.

questions.question: What is the National List of Essential Medicines? Write its significance.
questions.answer: Essential medicines satisfy priority health needs, chosen for efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness. India: lists in 1996, 2003, 2011, 2015 and 2022 (384 medicines, 27 categories). Listed by generic name with dosage form, strength and level of care. Significance: forms First Schedule of DPCO 2013 so these medicines are price-controlled; guides procurement, prescribing, education and insurance; promotes rational use and availability.

questions.question: Write the functions of the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority.
questions.answer: Set up 1997 under Department of Pharmaceuticals. Fixes and revises ceiling prices of scheduled formulations; fixes retail prices of new drugs; monitors prices of non-scheduled drugs (10% rule); enforces DPCO and recovers overcharged amounts with interest; monitors availability and shortages; collects data on production, import, sales; advises Government on pricing policy; handles public complaints.

questions.question: List the classes of advertisements exempted under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act.
questions.answer: Under s.14: signboard or notice of an RMP stating that treatment is given; treatise or book on the subject from a bona fide scientific or social standpoint; advertisement sent confidentially to RMPs, hospitals or laboratories marked for their use only; advertisement printed or published by Government or with its sanction; others exempted by Central Government notification.

questions.question: Define 'magic remedy'.
questions.answer: A talisman, mantra, kavacha, charm or any other article claimed to have miraculous power to cure, diagnose, prevent or mitigate disease or affect the structure or function of the body (DMR Act, 1954).

questions.question: What is a ceiling price?
questions.answer: The maximum price fixed by the Government under DPCO 2013 for a scheduled formulation; calculated as the simple average PTR of brands with at least 1% market share plus 16% retailer margin.

questions.question: Give a brief review of pharmaceutical legislation in India. Discuss the recommendations of the Drugs Enquiry Committee and the Hathi Committee.
questions.answer:
1. Need for laws: protect public from spurious drugs, quackery, misleading adverts, misuse of habit-forming drugs; set standards; control prices.
2. Timeline: Opium Acts 1857/1878, Poisons Act 1919, Dangerous Drugs Act 1930, Drugs Act 1940, Rules 1945, Pharmacy Act 1948, DMR Act 1954, M&TP Act 1955, PCA Act 1960, Patents Act 1970, MTP Act 1971, NDPS 1985, NPPA 1997, RTI 2005, DPCO 2013, NDCT Rules 2019.
3. Drugs Enquiry Committee (1930–31, Col. R. N. Chopra): found substandard/adulterated drugs and no control; recommended central drug law, CDL and provincial labs, drug control departments with inspectors, regulation of pharmacy profession, Indian pharmacopoeia → D&C Act 1940, Pharmacy Act 1948.
4. Hathi Committee (1974–75, Jaisukhlal Hathi, Committee on Drugs and Pharmaceutical Industry): list of 117 essential drugs; lead role for Indian and public sector; generic names with phased abolition of brand names; National Drug Authority; stronger quality and price control; research and bulk drug production → Drug Policy 1978.
5. Also mention Bhore (1943–46) and Mudaliar (1959–61) committees.

questions.question: What is a code of ethics? Discuss the code of pharmaceutical ethics with respect to the pharmacist in relation to his job, trade, medical profession and his profession. Add the pharmacist's oath.
questions.answer:
1. Definition: moral principles guiding conduct; PCI code of professional conduct; part of Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015.
2. Job: adequate opening hours and stock; clean premises; handle prescriptions correctly, no alteration without prescriber, contact prescriber on errors; accurate dispensing and labelling; care with poisons and narcotics; train apprentices; confidentiality.
3. Trade: fair prices within MRP/ceiling; no price wars or undercutting; no misleading adverts; fair dealing; no substandard or expired goods; no hawking; dignified display.
4. Medical profession: cooperate and respect; no counter-prescribing except first aid; no secret commission arrangements; no recommending doctors for gain; tactful correction of errors.
5. Profession: uphold dignity; continuing education; join associations; avoid discredit; help colleagues; obey laws.
6. Pharmacist's oath: service to humanity, relief of suffering, best use of knowledge, protect patient information, keep up to date, highest ethical and legal conduct, improve patient care, prevent misuse of medicines.

questions.question: Write an account of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 as amended in 2021.
questions.answer:
1. Objectives: safe legal termination by RMPs; reduce maternal deaths from unsafe abortion; specify when, where and by whom.
2. Definitions: RMP with gynaecology/obstetrics experience; guardian; termination of pregnancy.
3. Limits (2021, in force 24 Sept 2021): up to 20 weeks — one RMP; 20–24 weeks — two RMPs for notified special categories (rape survivors, minors, change of marital status, disability etc.); beyond 24 weeks — substantial foetal abnormalities by State Medical Board; any time to save life.
4. Grounds: risk to life or grave injury to physical/mental health; risk of serious abnormality; rape presumed grave mental injury; contraceptive failure of any woman or partner.
5. Consent: woman's written consent; guardian for minor or mentally ill woman.
6. Place: Government hospital or approved place.
7. s.5A confidentiality — up to 1 year imprisonment or fine or both; termination by non-RMP punishable under criminal law (BNS).
8. Pharmacist: MTP drugs (mifepristone, misoprostol) only on RMP prescription with records.

questions.question: Write the salient features of the Right to Information Act, 2005.
questions.answer:
1. Right of citizens to information held by public authorities (records, e-mails, samples, electronic data).
2. Application to PIO with fee ₹10 (Central), BPL exempt; no reasons needed.
3. Reply within 30 days; 48 hours for life or liberty; +5 days via APIO.
4. First appeal to senior officer within 30 days; second appeal to Central/State Information Commission within 90 days.
5. Section 8 exemptions (security, court bar, privilege, trade secrets, fiduciary, personal information etc.); security agencies excluded (s.24) except corruption/human rights.
6. Penalty on PIO ₹250/day up to ₹25,000.
7. s.4 proactive disclosure.

questions.question: What are intellectual property rights? Write a note on patents with respect to pharmaceuticals.
questions.answer: IPR: legal rights over creations of the mind for limited time — patents, trademarks, copyright, designs, GI, trade secrets; TRIPS (WTO 1995). Patents Act 1970: 20 years from filing; criteria novelty, inventive step, industrial application; 1970 process patents only for drugs; product patents from 2005; s.3(d) new forms of known substances need enhanced efficacy (Novartis 2013); pre- and post-grant opposition; s.84 compulsory licence after 3 years (Natco–Bayer sorafenib 2012); s.107A Bolar exemption. Balances R&D reward and access to medicines.

questions.question: Write short notes on the Health Survey and Development Committee and the Mudaliar Committee.
questions.answer: Bhore Committee (Health Survey and Development, appointed 1943, reported 1946, Sir Joseph Bhore): surveyed health system; integrate preventive and curative care; primary health centres; train health personnel including pharmacists; local drug production; drug control. Mudaliar Committee (Health Survey and Planning, 1959–61, Dr A. L. Mudaliar): reviewed progress; strengthen PHCs; improve pharmacy education and status; strengthen Central and State drug control; regional drug-testing laboratories; indigenous drug production.

questions.question: Compare the main types of intellectual property rights in India.
questions.answer: Patent (Patents Act 1970) — inventions, 20 years. Trademark (Trade Marks Act 1999) — brand names and logos, 10 years renewable. Copyright (Copyright Act 1957) — literary, artistic works, software, life + 60 years. Design (Designs Act 2000) — shape and appearance, 10 + 5 years. Geographical indication (GI Act 1999) — goods linked to a place, 10 years renewable. Trade secret — confidential know-how, protected by contract as long as secret.

questions.question: Who chaired the Drugs Enquiry Committee and what did it lead to?
questions.answer: Col. R. N. Chopra (1930–31); its report led to the Drugs Act, 1940 (now Drugs and Cosmetics Act) and later the Pharmacy Act, 1948.

questions.question: What is section 3(d) of the Patents Act?
questions.answer: It states that a new form of a known substance (salt, ester, polymorph, isomer etc.) is not patentable unless it shows significantly enhanced efficacy; upheld in the Novartis (imatinib) case, 2013.
